However, the solution cannot be commercialized as it is not compatible with current products, e.g., onboard chargers. STRIVE will bridge the compatibility gap and unleash the deployment of this superior EV architecture.

Project Title: Making Accessible Media with Youth: Advancing Disability and Access
Project Description: Ontario youth with disabilities are becoming world leaders in making accessible media. Their online content production is creative, compelling, and has proven to change people’s attitudes toward disability. With the implementation deadline for the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act (2025) nearing, this project elevates Ontario youth’s access-forward communication practices that go beyond compliance—their skills are vast, vibrant, and uncontainable by “best practices” checklists. By measuring how standards are currently taken up in Ontario post-secondary media programs, this project mobilizes four free online “RelaxComm” Summer Institutes to train and mentor 60 young content creators from around the world in Ontario-based accessible media production. The Summer Institutes, rooted in Ontario disabled youth’s “relaxed” approach to accessibility, are supported by a network of international mentors from Canada, the United States, and Australia, as well as 12 highly qualified Ontario-based personnel uniquely trained as Access Activators with expertise in ethical practice—a postdoctoral fellow, a research associate, and graduate students. In consultation with a 10-person Youth Advisory Committee, the team will produce a publicly available co-authored report recommending new accessibility standards and formats in information and communication policy with impact provincially, nationally, and internationally.
Keywords: Accessible media, children and youth, communications, disability media studies, disability studies, critical access, critical digital pedagogy, relaxed performance, RelaxPed, disability representation

Project Title: Understanding and Addressing Technology-Facilitated Sexual Offences in Ontario
Project Description:
The proposed research will address the rise of technology-facilitated sexual offences in Ontario, including nonconsensual forwarding of sexts and sextortion, and the crossover from online child sexual exploitation material (CSEM) to in-person sexual offences. These offences have surged with increasing internet use and sexting, straining Ontario's criminal justice system.

To tackle these issues, the research will identify factors linked to these offences. In Objective 1 and 2, a longitudinal survey of 800 university students will identify the predictors of victimization and perpetration of nonconsensual forwarding and sextortion. In Objective 3, data from a cohort of 800 CSEM offenders, collected through my existing partnerships with Ontario Corrections and Ontario Provincial Police, will be analyzed to detect factors that predict which CSEM offenders cross-over to commit in-person sexual offences.  

The benefits to Ontario are substantial. The findings will inform prevention programs and sexual education curricula for schools and universities, reducing the incidence of these offences. The insight gained will also enhance the management of sex offenders in Ontario, helping prioritize resources, enhancing public safety, and reducing the burden on the criminal justice system. Ultimately, the research will contribute to safer communities and lower the societal costs associated with sexual offences in Ontario.
Keywords: Technology-facilitated sexual offences; Child sexual exploitation material; Nonconsensual forwarding; Sextortion; Risk assessment; Prevention; Correctional outcomes

Project Title: Synergies and trade-offs between human health and biodiversity outcomes of nature-based solutions in Ontario cities
Project Description: Biodiversity loss is accelerating, and concurrently, rates of mental illness are on the rise. Urban living exacerbates these intertwined crises, which are particularly pressing in heavily urbanized southern Ontario. Nature-based solutions— interventions that work with nature to provide multiple benefits—hold the potential to tackle these two challenges simultaneously. Although policymakers across Canadian cities have demonstrated a growing interest in nature-based solutions, the outcomes for biodiversity and human health, including the trade-offs and synergies between these domains, remain poorly understood. Building on the biodiversity-focused research program I have established at Carleton University, my HQP and I will use an interdisciplinary approach to assess the outcomes of nature-based solutions and explore how to bring these interventions to scale. We will: 1) explore the outcomes of reducing traffic in urban parks for wildlife and human visitors, including visitors with limited mobility; 2) evaluate the co-benefits of tree planting in urban areas for mental health and biodiversity; and 3) identify locations to scale up urban nature-based solutions in Ontario cities to benefit people’s health, as well as biodiversity. We will work with practitioners and policymakers to guide more effective nature-based solutions in Ontario while building capacity through HQP training and outreach.
Keywords: biodiversity; birds; cities; co-benefits; mental health; nature-based solutions; synergies; trade-offs; urban

Project Title: Decarbonizing Steel and Auto Manufacturing Industries in Ontario
Project Description: Ontario is at the heart of Canada’s metal and auto manufacturing. However, production of metals and their use in cars has a significant carbon footprint: >2 tons of CO2 per ton of steel and >5.6 tons of CO2 per ton of aluminum. Significant amounts of scrap metal waste that cannot easily be recycled are produced during metal and auto manufacturing. These industries must reduce their emissions and waste to stay competitive in Ontario. The steel industry must provide 50% of Ontario’s commitment of 12,000,000 tonnes of CO2 emissions reductions by 2030. The auto industry has a mandate to source its metals from low-emission vendors. This project develops technologies that oxidize waste scrap metal from various manufacturing processes with air, water or CO2 to produce emission-free energy, green hydrogen, syngas and valuable metal oxide commodities. Reactivity of samples from industry partners will be investigated to obtain optimum process conditions for maximum yield and desired particle properties. Techno-economic and life cycle analysis will be performed to quantify economic and emission reduction benefits of such technologies for Ontario. Adopting such technologies and their products could significantly reduce the carbon footprint and cost of manufacturing processes by heavy industries in Ontario.
Keywords: Scrap Aluminum, Scrap Iron, Steel Manufacturing Metallic Waste, Auto Manufacturing  Metallic Waste, Low Carbon Hydrogen, Metal Fuels, Metal Oxides, Carbon Dioxide Conversion

Project Title: Disrupting sex steroid hormones in young women
Project Description: In Ontario, the burden of depression (measured in years of life lost and years of reduced functioning) is more than the combined burden of lung, colorectal, breast, and prostate cancers. While the causes are complex, women are twice as likely to suffer from depression than men, and significant evidence points to the involvement of sex steroid hormones, such as estrogen. It is surprising then that more than 100 million women worldwide use hormone contraceptives, which affect natural levels of estrogen, and progesterone, without fully understanding their influence. The lack of evidence on how hormone contraceptives affect women’s brains, bodies and behaviours is one of the most striking oversights in neuroscience history. To correct this oversight, my ERA research will examine the short and long-term effects of hormone contraceptives on neurobiology, stress physiology, and mental health among young women. These findings could inform medical recommendations for specific hormonal contraceptives, allowing young women to make evidence-based decisions about their health. Moreover, this proposal will help elucidate the role of sex steroid hormones in depression, potentially contributing to more effective and tailored treatments in Ontario, which is needed as current pharmacological treatments are effective in less than 50% of individuals with depression.
FOR - Level 3 Class Title: Neurosciences, medical and physiological and health aspects
Keywords: Cortisol, Estrogen, Epigenetics, Depression, Hormone Contraceptives, Inflammation, Mental health, Sex hormones, Stress, Women

Project Title: Improving food allergy care using allergen thresholds
Project Description: Food allergy is a growing problem affecting over 7% of Ontarians and 1 in 2 households. Food allergic reactions and management costs Ontario's economy $16.4 billion annually directly (healthcare utilization, patient expenses) and indirectly (lost productivity, schooling, and time). Current experimental treatments that desensitize food allergy, called immunotherapy, cause significant adverse effects. Hence, how to best manage food allergy is unclear. I propose an  Ontario multicentre registry study (TITAN) to define how much allergen needs to be eaten in order to trigger an allergic reaction, critical to understanding food safety, and identify ways to predict allergy sensitivity and reactivity. For patients in TITAN identified as food allergic, I propose a placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial (TRADE) to evaluate two new treatments employing immunotherapy at doses that could have beneficial effects and little to no adverse effects. TITAN could improve patient safety and provide evidence-based safe allergen levels for food manufacturers/industry. The Ontario TRADE clinical trial could transform standards of care in food allergy with two new treatments. By decreasing reactions, emergency room and physician visits, lost productivity, and improving quality of life, these projects have the potential to improve the outcomes of Ontarians with food allergy and alleviate its economic burden.
Keywords: food allergy; treatment and management; diagnosis; randomized clinical trials; prognosis; registry; evidence-based medicine; clinical research; improving outcomes; patient and family engagement

Project Title: Advancing Affordable Housing in Ontario Using Resilient Additively Manufactured Homes
Project Description: Recent reports by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation demonstrated that the housing stock-to-population ratio in Ontario is rapidly declining and the province needs an additional 1.48 million housing units by 2030 to restore affordability. The current shortage of affordable housing is disproportionately borne by youth, Indigenous, and racialized communities in Ontario. This housing crisis is partly attributed to the fact that construction remains largely a manually intensive process, whereas many other industries have made significant progress in the use of digital and automation technologies. The proposed research will empower digital and mobile construction in Ontario by developing ready-to-use construction techniques for additively manufactured (AM) concrete homes. To provide our communities with resilient housing, this research will employ advanced experimental and computational techniques such as artificial intelligence tools to quantify the performance of such structures under severe environmental conditions and extreme seismic scenarios. The public and private sectors will directly benefit from the research outcomes by promoting equal affordable housing opportunities. As the field of AM concrete structures is still in its infancy in terms of standardization, this research will facilitate knowledge mobilization from academia to industrial applications and position Ontario as a world leader in this emerging construction field.
FOR - Level 2 Group Title: Civil engineering, maritime engineering, transport engineering, and mining engineering
Keywords: Additive Manufacturing; Concrete; Data-driven; Durability; Dynamic Loading; Earthquakes; Hazards; Housing; Predictive Models; Resilience

Project Title: Using rehabilitation to improve outcomes in Ontarians with a history of cancer
Project Description: Individuals with a cancer diagnosis are living longer. However, survivors of cancer live with physical and psychosocial sequalae affecting their overall function, quality of life, and ability to return to pre-cancer activities. As the number of Ontarians living with a cancer diagnosis increases, research and clinical focus must be centered on managing the persistent limitations of this population. Rehabilitation has known benefits for individuals living with cancer, however access and engagement is low. This program of research is focused on 1) implementing physical activity and exercise for individuals with a current or past diagnosis of cancer within cancer institutions across Ontario, and 2) using technology to detect upper extremity impairment early in those with a history of cancer. In the first research arm we are conducting a full-scale implementation-effectiveness trial using randomized controlled trial methodology in 129 participants at five cancer centers across Ontario to measure functional outcomes and cost-effectiveness over five years. In the second arm we are creating and testing an mHealth system (StrongArms-Cancer) to prevent, track, and manage upper extremity complications in survivors of cancer. These projects represent innovative contributions to cancer research and have direct relevance on improving the lives of individuals with cancer in Ontario.
Keywords: cancer, oncology, rehabilitation, exercise, physical activity, self-management, self-care, function, technology, implementation science

Project Title: Generative AI for novel antibiotic design against drug-resistant bacterial pathogens
Project Description: Antibiotic resistance is a global threat to public health. In 2019, approximately 1.3 million deaths were caused globally by antibiotic-resistant infections. In 2018, it is estimated that over 25% of bacterial infections in Canada were resistant to at least one first-line antibiotic, and that 14,000 Canadian deaths were associated with antibiotic resistance. In Ontario, on average, the number of drug-resistant bacterial infections has tripled since the early 2000s, from ~5% to upwards of 15%. To increase the rate of development of novel antibiotics, we must invent innovative methods that increase the efficiency of this process. Here, we will develop and apply state-of-the-art generative AI models to design novel antibiotics against the ESKAPE pathogens – a group of burdensome bacterial species that are responsible for the overwhelming majority of antibiotic-resistant infections. This will be achieved through (a) developing reinforcement learning-based generative AI models; (b) developing language-based generative AI models; and (c) using both architectures to design novel antibitoics that will be synthesized and tested in the laboratory. This leading-edge research will attract HQP, accelerate the Ontario biotechnology sector by providing the province with novel antibacterial molecules with strong translational potential, and help relieve the burden of drug-resistant infections on Ontario healthcare systems.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, machine learning, reinforcement learning, chemical language model, drug discovery, microbiology, antibiotic discovery, antibiotic resistance

Project Title: Integrated Multi-layer Traffic Prediction and Management with Connected and Automated Vehicles
Project Description:
According to the Ontario Ministry of Transportation (MTO), road congestion currently costs Ontario’s economy over $11 billion annually in lost productivity. Moreover, travel time on most major freeways in Ontario is projected to increase by 44% between 2016 and 2051. This research aims to solve two critical challenges: real-time traffic monitoring and efficient traffic management, to enhance transportation services in Ontario. To achieve this goal, an AI platform will be developed to monitor and manage road transportation using connected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs) and AI/machine learning technologies for city-level road networks in cities like Hamilton and Toronto. The platform will utilize multi-source data collected by CAVs to monitor and predict traffic conditions and train AI-based CAV control to mitigate gridlock.
For the first time, this research will create an AI and CAV-enabled platform that integrates real-time traffic estimation, prediction, and multi-layer traffic management for Ontario road networks. In the long term, the system will assist both public and private transportation entities in Ontario to collaboratively deploy innovative CAV applications in large cities. It will also support MTO’s Greater Golden Horseshoe (GGH) plan to alleviate congestion and enhance the movement of people and goods.
FOR - Level 2 Group Title: Civil engineering, maritime engineering, transport engineering, and mining engineering
Keywords: Connected and automated vehicles, AI and machine learning, traffic estimation and prediction, large-scale network management, road congestion mitigation, mobility services, real-time traffic control

Project Title: Discovering general principles for strongly interacting metals
Project Description:
Metals are a commonly encountered state of matter. Metals in which the physics is dominated by strong interactions between electrons are known as “non-Fermi liquids”. They remain poorly understood theoretically, and many striking experimental observations, such as electrical resistivity that varies linearly with temperature, have not yet been explained.

In this project, we will adopt a new strategy. Rather than seeking to develop particular models of non-Fermi liquids, we will endeavour to identify the general principles and constraints that *all* metals must satisfy. This will build on my previous work establishing general properties of metals using modern methods in strongly interacting quantum field theories. A focus will be on developing the concept of “holography” into a theoretical laboratory to test general principles.

The project is expected to yield a more systematic understanding of the theoretical possibilities for non-Fermi liquid metals, ultimately allowing for direct comparisons with experiment. It will increase the profile of theoretical condensed matter physics research in Ontario. The project will train two PhD students in modern and innovative methods in condensed matter physics, and in broadly applicable quantitative skills, preparing them for successful careers in academia or industries including artificial intelligence, quantum information, or finance.
FOR - Level 4 Sub-Class Title: Electronic and magnetic properties of condensed matter and supraconductivity
Keywords: Strongly interacting quantum many-body systems, Metals, Non-Fermi liquid metals, Strange metals, Holography, T-linear resistivity, Emergent symmetries, Fermi surfaces

Project Title: Advanced computer simulations to study zirconium for Ontario nuclear reactors
Project Description:
Ontario's nuclear reactors, which provide nearly 60% of the province's electricity, rely on zirconium (Zr) alloys for key components. However, these materials face challenges from radiation and hydrogen exposure, which can lead to structural issues like deformation and cracking of reactor pressure tubes. My research aims to use advanced computer simulations to understand how these problems occur at the atomic level. By studying the behavior of nanoscale defects and hydrogen atoms within Zr alloys, we can predict how these materials will behave over time under reactor conditions.
The insights gained will help improve the design and maintenance of reactor components, making Ontario's nuclear reactors safer and more efficient. Additionally, this research will train new experts in cutting-edge computational techniques, who will be highly valuable to Ontario's nuclear industry. The outcomes will not only support Ontario's energy sector but also enhance the province's position as a leader in advanced materials science and technology. By addressing these critical issues, we contribute to the safe and sustainable future of Ontario's nuclear power.
FOR - Level 4 Sub-Class Title: Condensed matter modeling and density functional theory
Keywords: materials modeling; atomistic simulations; machine learning; computational materials science; nuclear materials; zirconium hydrides; radiation effects

Project Title: Rhizobium inoculants for Ontario adzuki bean and soybean crops
Project Description: Over 40% of Ontario’s seeded crop land is used to grow legumes. Legumes are climate-smart crops able to associate with nitrogen-fixing bacteria (called rhizobia) that can eliminate the need for nitrogen fertilizer. However, there are no commercially available rhizobium products to support the nutrition of the high value crop adzuki bean, while there is a risk that existing inoculants for the widely grown soybean crop will lose effectiveness. Developing new rhizobium products will ensure Ontario growers can grow these important crops with limited chemical inputs, thereby keeping grower costs low, promoting national food security, and limiting the production of greenhouse gases. To accomplish this, we will collect 100s of rhizobia from Ontario soils able to associate with Ontario cultivars of adzuki bean and soybean. We will screen these bacteria for their ability to fulfill the nitrogen requirements of these crops in greenhouse conditions, with field trials subsequently undertaken using the top-performing strains. Effective strains will be made available to growers through partnering with Canadian-based inoculant companies or through establishing Ontario-based start-ups. We will additionally monitor the effectiveness of current soybean inoculants, providing growers crucial information to allow them to make informed nutrient management decisions.
Keywords: Rhizobia; legumes; symbiotic nitrogen fixation; nodulation; plant-microbe interactions; whole genome sequencing; comparative genomics; environmental microbiology, plant-growth promoting rhizobacteria; bacteriology

Project Title: Integrated carbon capture and conversion to fuels and chemicals
Project Description:
Capturing the greenhouse gas CO2 and converting it into useful chemicals and fuels using renewable energy (carbon utilization) are the focus of intense research worldwide because they are crucial tools for limiting global warming by sequestering emissions from hard-to-decarbonize sources. The renewable fuels resulting from this process can also serve as stable energy storage for variable wind and solar power, which reduces the need for grid-level battery capacity. The proposed research will increase the practical viability of these technologies by integrating CO2 capture with electrochemical conversion to produce chemicals directly from the CO2 capture solution, thus eliminating one particularly energy-intensive step. It will also explore several innovative approaches to optimize system efficiency, longevity, and selective production of specific chemicals. 

This research program will support Ontario's CO2 emission reduction goals by reducing reliance on fossil-based fuels in transportation and other industries that account for 65% of Ontario's greenhouse gas emissions. It will also create opportunities for an emerging carbon capture and utilization industry, for which Ontario is ideally suited due to its comparatively low-carbon electricity supply. Additionally, this program will train and prepare Highly Qualified Personnel for CO2 reduction research leadership in academia and Ontario’s clean tech industry.
Keywords: CO2 capture and utilization, renewable fuels and chemicals, electrochemical conversion, sustainability, electrocatalysis, CO2 conversion

Project Title: The Onset of Planet Formation Around Young Stars
Project Description: Planets form in disks of dust and gas around young stars.  Many late-stage disks show structures such as gaps with less material and bright rings with more material.  Understanding how and when these disks become structured is key to determining when planets begin to form and the types of planets that will be produced.  If these features are sites where planets are born, then the conditions for forming planets arises early in the disk lifetime during the protostellar stage.  But only a handful of very young protostellar disks have had detected structure to date.  With this ERA grant, my team and I will use observations and simulations of young, protostellar disks in nearby star-forming regions to identify which disks have structure, measure their physical properties, and test different theoretical predictions for structure formation.  This grant will train students in data acquisition and analysis techniques that include the development of sophisticated 2-D and 3-D models of young disks.  We will use these models to study how protostellar disks become structured and the connection of these structures to planets.  We will further determine under which conditions these could produce an Earth-Moon system and test theories about the formation  of our Solar System.
Keywords: star formation, planet formation, interstellar dust, circumstellar disks, interferometry, radiative transfer models, synthetic observations

Project Title: Preventing falls in Ontario using bio-inspired trunk exoskeletons
Project Description: Falls are the greatest cause of injury-related hospitalization within Ontario (Public Health Ontario 2022). Falls lower quality of life by decreasing mobility and are a direct barrier to older adults, the fastest growing age group in Ontario, and their desire to age independently in their homes or community. My project aims to prevent falls by (1) investigating gait stability of healthy adults in real-world environments and (2) developing a trunk exoskeleton that can detect and mitigate fall risk. We will conduct key human studies to evaluate how the trunk affects gait and integrate study findings into the development of a trunk exoskeleton controller that can provide indirect (haptic) or direct (active) assistance. Our proposed research has significant health, social, and economic value to Ontario. Fall prevention will enhance the well-being of older adults and support Ontario Health’s new "aging care continuum plan" (Annual Business Plan 2023/24). Reduced occurrence of fall-related hospital visits will ease healthcare costs and bolster Ontario Ministry of Health’s priority to reduce preventable emergency room visits. In addition, trainees’ advanced skillset in biomechanics and robotics will equip them to become leaders in the growing robotics and health technology industries, areas of strategic value to Ontario.
Keywords: balance, locomotion, stability, exoskeleton, bio-inspired control, human-robot interaction, mechanics, energetics, haptic feedback, perturbations

Project Title: Pan-cancer quantification of immunosuppressive cell states by large-scale single-cell analysis
Project Description: The immune system is the first line of defense against cancer cells, but its ability to attack them is often severely impaired. Immunotherapies are recent therapeutic breakthroughs that reverse this immunosuppression; however, its exact causes remain unknown, limiting our ability to effectively target it to treat various forms of cancer. Recent technological advances have produced an abundance of data on the gene expression patterns of single cells from human cancers. This information can be used to reveal the specific roles of these cells, raising the tantalizing possibility of using patient samples to identify which human cell types contribute to immunosuppression in cancer for the first time. Here, we will develop and apply cutting-edge computational methods to map and compare the cell types promoting immunosuppression across eight different cancers. We will compare our findings between the sexes and investigate whether they are linked to patient responses to immunotherapy. Finally, we will develop machine learning approaches to prioritize novel therapeutic targets that can alleviate tumour immunosuppression. This research will provide new insights into fundamental cancer biology, deliver sought-after training in artificial intelligence and biomedical data analysis, and identify potential drug targets for future commercialization.
Keywords: machine learning, single-cell, tumour microenvironment, immunotherapy, immunosuppression, gene expression

Project Title: Studying the EffecTiveness of SGLT2 InHibitoRs on PallIative Outcomes in AdVancEd Heart Failure: The THRIVE-HF Collaborative
Project Description: Heart failure (HF) is a life-limiting condition associated with poor quality of life, burdensome symptoms, and high healthcare needs. Each year, an estimated 100,000 Canadians are diagnosed with HF, and 750,000 live with it. Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) are a novel class of medications that provide several benefits to adults with HF, including reducing the risk of hospitalization. However, lack of knowledge about their potential benefits and harms in people with advanced HF nearing end-of-life has limited their use in these vulnerable patients. In addition, these drugs could be useful palliative care interventions in regions with limited palliative care resources, such as rural Ontario. In this research, we will use cutting-edge approaches to define how SGLT2is impact the quality of life and healthcare usage of multimorbid Ontarians with advanced HF at end-of-life. This work will inform clinical practice, health policy, and the design of a pragmatic multicentre randomized clinical trial. This will conserve valuable healthcare resources and improve the care of the many Ontarians living with advanced HF.
Keywords: advanced heart failure, sodium glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, end-of-life care, palliative care, quality of life, survival, health services research, patient safety

Project Title: Increasing Initiation of Diabetes Technologies Among Socially Disadvantaged Adults with Type 1 Diabetes through Patient- and Provider-Level Behaviour Change
Project Description: Advanced diabetes technologies like insulin pumps and continuous glucose monitoring devices are the most effective tools to help people manage life with type 1 diabetes. These technologies prevent life-limiting and expensive complications and should be readily accessible to all who are willing and able to use them appropriately. However, both financial and non-financial barriers make individuals with social disadvantage (e.g., low income, visible minority, language barrier) less likely to initiate diabetes technologies, contributing to worse diabetes outcomes. We are currently conducting a three-phase research project (EQUAT1D) that will develop strategies for increasing the initiation of diabetes technologies among adults with type 1 diabetes who are socially disadvantaged via specific tools for patients and their providers. This research will build on the EQUAT1D study, progressing it to a pivotal next stage: developing the specific clinical tools used in the program, then evaluating its feasibility and potential clinical effectiveness with a randomized controlled trial. This research will inform a larger definitive trial and influence health policy and clinical practice for type 1 diabetes in Ontario, leading to more equitable outcomes and saving healthcare costs.
Keywords: Type 1 Diabetes, Diabetes Technologies, Health Disparities, Randomized Controlled Trial, Feasibility Trial, Patient-Oriented Research, Implementation Research

Project Title: Artificial intelligence for guiding treatment decisions in acute ischemic stroke
Project Description:
Stroke is a leading cause of death worldwide, with a significant societal and economic burden, including substantial healthcare costs and long-term disabilities for survivors. Current methods for identifying stroke severity and guiding endovascular treatment (EVT) are limited by their accuracy, processing times, and reliance on multiple imaging modalities prone to errors. Our project aims to revolutionize acute ischemic stroke care through advanced AI and deep learning models, addressing critical challenges in patient selection and treatment efficacy by developing three AI-based models: 
1. A segmentation model to precisely delineate stroke core and penumbra using multi-phase CT angiography and non-contrast CT data.
2. A generative model to synthesize CT perfusion maps from CT angiography and non-contrast CT, providing comprehensive perfusion information crucial for treatment decisions.
3. A predictive model integrating clinical data and imaging features to guide EVT patient selection, enhancing outcomes prediction.

Based on a very large dataset (>6,000 scans) from Sunnybrook Hospital, these models aim to improve accuracy, streamline workflow, and reduce time-to-treatment, thereby benefiting a large number of stroke patients across Ontario. This research will significantly impact clinical practice in Ontario, including enhanced treatment decisions, reduced healthcare costs, and expanded capabilities for stroke management beyond specialized centres.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, stroke, medical imaging, CT, endovascular treatment, image segmentation, image generation, predictive modelling

Project Title: Improving Corneal Transplant Outcomes and Developing Next Generation Therapeutics for Ontarians
Project Description: In Ontario, approximately 3.5% of the population is affected by vision loss, which includes diseases that affect the cornea, the transparent front part of the eye that allows us to see. My research focuses on Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy (FECD), a progressive age-related disease with a female predilection that is the leading cause of corneal dysfunction, and the top indication for corneal transplantation worldwide and Ontario. My proposal aims to (1) improve corneal transplantation outcomes using a novel surgical delivery device that results in ready-to-use corneal transplantation tissue prepared by the Eye Bank of Canada – Ontario division, and (2) optimize Descemet’s stripping only (DSO), a new surgical technique that regenerates the corneal endothelium without a corneal transplant. This will have an immediate impact on Ontario patients requiring a corneal transplant as all corneal surgeons in Ontario will be able to use eye bank prepared corneal transplantation tissue to help improve surgical efficiency and operating room utilization, thus reducing surgical wait time (9 months) and allowing more patients to undergo timely surgery. Furthermore, my work to develop a novel therapeutic for DSO, will reduce healthcare costs in Ontario associated with corneal transplantation, and it has commercialization potential.
FOR - Level 3 Class Title: Neurosciences, medical and physiological and health aspects
Keywords: Cornea, transplantation, Fuchs dystrophy, regeneration, aging, vision , DMEK, DSO, cell migration

Project Title: From Heart to Brain: The Influence of Cardiovascular Health and Menopause Timing on Dementia Risk in Women from Ontario
Project Description:
In Ontario, over 250,000 people have dementia. Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia and disproportionately affects women, accounting for over two-thirds of cases. This sex disparity remains poorly understood. 

Vascular conditions like hypertension and obesity increase the risk of AD, with women becoming more vulnerable to these conditions after menopause. Menopause triggers a decline in estrogen, a sex hormone vital for brain health. The negative effects of menopause on brain function are more severe if menopause begins at an earlier age. Despite this, the combined impact of earlier menopause and poor vascular health on AD risk is not well understood.

This study aims to investigate how the timing of menopause and vascular health collectively influence brain and cognitive health in women in Ontario. We will also examine the modifying effects of hormone therapy and genetic factors. As such, this research seeks to uncover sex-specific mechanisms underlying AD to develop more tailored prevention and intervention strategies. By addressing this critical knowledge gap, we aim to combat the rising tide of dementia in Ontario and beyond, offering hope for effective, personalized approaches to women's brain health.
FOR - Level 3 Class Title: Neurosciences, medical and physiological and health aspects
Keywords: Dementia, Alzheimer's disease, Women's health, Menopause, Cerebrovascular disease, Cardiovascular disease Cognitive Impairment, Genetics, APOE, BDNF

Project Title: Interventional Psychiatry Research Program: Pioneering Procedural Treatments in Mental Health
Project Description: About 1.14M Ontarians with depression do not respond to standard antidepressant treatments, thus have a condition known as difficult-to-treat depression (DTD). People with DTD experience challenges that limit their ability to perform day-to-day activities, face barriers to their meaningful participation in society, and are at risk of death by suicide. New procedural treatments, including inhaled or infused medications and brain stimulation, have the potential to help, but must first be examined in a controlled research environment to determine how well they work and for which types of patients. Our project will create a comprehensive research program to investigate procedural treatments that alleviate depressive symptoms in DTD. Our research will provide evidence that supports the use of procedural treatments for DTD, reduce the number of resistant cases, determine which patients will benefit from which treatment, and ultimately improve the lives of persons living with depressive symptoms.
Keywords: Interventional Psychiatry, procedural treatments, ketamine, nitrous oxide, rTMS, depression

Project Title: Indigenous and racialized women's wellbeing matters: Addressing sedentarism and commitment to physical activity
Project Description:
The proposed research aims to improve the health equity of Indigenous and racialized women by engaging in innovative research about physical activity. This project targets physical inactivity, a risk factor contributing to chronic diseases, with the goal of reducing health and economic burdens in Ontario. To identify best practices for Ontario, Indigenous and racialized women’s sedentarism and commitment to physical activity will be studied through training in martial arts. HOW RESEARCH ADDRESSES ISSUES: This project will employ a trauma-informed physical activity approach in martial arts using an Indigenous research framework to increase physical activity participation rates among participants. This project aims to mitigate the burden of chronic diseases, reduce hospital overcrowding, and improve overall health outcomes by addressing sedentarism. BENEFITS TO ONTARIO: The project will bring great economic and social benefits to Ontario. Chronic diseases are driven mainly by physical inactivity, which costs Ontario $2.6 billion annually in direct and indirect healthcare costs. Relatedly, the economic burden of sedentarism leads to a loss of productivity, placing a financial burden on families and communities. These alarming trends will be addressed in this proposal through a culturally informed and community-based approach, which promotes physical activity while respecting traditional knowledge and values. 

My proposed research will develop guidance for meta-analyzing rare events. Meta-analysis, used by organizations like Health Quality Ontario, integrates multiple study findings for thorough intervention assessments. However, common meta-analytic methods are unsuitable for rare events and can lead to biased estimates and poor decision-making, potentially compromising patient safety. Previous research has highlighted major uncertainties in methods for rare events, impacting conclusions’ reliability and validity. 

My research will review and test these methods, identify gaps, and provide consensus-driven recommendations for optimal meta-analytic approaches. Enhanced evidence assessment leads to more effective clinical trials, aligning with Clinical Trials Ontario's goals. This research will help Ontario Health make informed decision-making for improved health outcomes of Ontarians and beyond.
FOR - Level 4 Sub-Class Title: Sociology and social studies of health, health systems and health care
Keywords: women, health, sociocultural, sedentarism, mental health, physical activity, martial arts, Indigenous research

Project Title: Optimized heat adaptation infrastructure for liveable and equitable Ontario cities
Project Description: Extreme heat is among the deadliest of natural hazards and is projected to more than triple in frequency over the coming decades in many Ontario cities, where 80% of Ontarians live. Variations in urban design lead heat exposure to differ considerably between neighbourhoods; however, its variation is often inadequately assessed. We will apply high resolution urban datasets and our recent developments within a state-of-the-art regional climate model to capture variation of heat exposure within and between neighbourhoods in Toronto and London, Ontario, based on physiologically-relevant combinations of air temperature, humidity, wind, and radiation exposures. This analysis has not been performed elsewhere and will revolutionize heat vulnerability mapping. A novel suite of our lab’s climate model developments will subsequently be applied to determine optimal combinations of heat adaptation infrastructure, such as green roofs, street trees and cool materials, that reduce heat exposure in each neighborhood. We will also quantify the environmental equity implications of targeting heat vulnerable neighbourhoods in both cities with this optimized infrastructure. The proposed work will provide world-class HQP training, key insights applicable to other Ontario cities, and put heat adaptation in Ontario on the international map by applying the most advanced modelling tools available.
Keywords: Extreme Heat; Urban Heat Islands; Urban Design for Heat Adaptation; Climate Change Impacts; Thermal Comfort; Environmental Equity; Regional Climate Modelling; Passive Cooling; Green Infrastructure; Heat Vulnerability

Project Title: Weaving Indigenous Knowledge and Western Science for More Effective and Collaborative Moose Monitoring and Research in Ontario
Project Description: Indigenous-led research programs created in partnership among Indigenous and non-Indigenous environmental professionals offer a promising context to bring together Indigenous Knowledge and Western science to solve complex environmental issues. While there are several theoretical frameworks that outline how to work well across cultures, very few resources detail how to do so in practice, leading to a general uncertainty of how to move forward in meaningful ways. Finding ways to work well across cultures is particularly important in Ontario for species in decline within the province that are valuable to all residents. The Ontario Ministry of Indigenous Affairs Priority Outcomes (2023-2024) describe the need to “Enhance awareness and best practices for consulting or engaging with Indigenous people, including the development and sharing of tools and guidance to support consistent and coordinated approaches across government.” Moose (Alces alces), a species that has been in decline over several decades within the province, provide an opportunity to establish a time-sensitive, culturally relevant case study to create monitoring and research programs founded in Indigenous and Western scientific knowledge systems. By working together in good ways, moose, the land, and the residents of Ontario who rely upon the environment, all benefit substantially.
Keywords: Indigenous environmental science, Indigenous Knowledge, Weaving Knowledge Systems, Wildlife management, Natural resources, Ethical Space, Wildlife monitoring, Indigenous Guardians, Moose (Alces alces), Socioecological research

Project Title: Bridging the Gap: Enhancing Traffic Safety through innovative data methodologies
Project Description: Several Canadian cities have adopted Vision-Zero Road Safety Plans aimed at eliminating traffic fatalities by designing safer road systems. These plans, which include the implementation of traffic calming measures, recognize human error and view traffic deaths as preventable. However, comprehensive evaluations of these strategies are lacking, and disparities exist in their distribution across socioeconomic areas. Previous research into traffic calming measures across various municipalities have uncovered a lack of precise data on the implementation dates and location. Moreover, these interventions can change traffic volume and road user types, necessitating granular data on traffic volume for robust evaluations. This project will address these gaps using innovative data collection methods, including machine learning for object detection and navigation data for traffic volume. The proposed approach, combining rigorous methodologies and interdisciplinary partnerships, aims to enhance scientific knowledge, influence public policy, and promote safer environments amid shifting transportation modes in Ontario and Canada.
FOR - Level 4 Sub-Class Title: Environmental and occupational health and safety
Keywords: Road traffic collisions, Injury, Active Transportation, Social Determinants, Built Environment, Causal Inference, Image Recognition

Project Title: Enhancing vaccine access into lymph nodes using dynamic DNA materials
Project Description:
In Ontario, cancer and infectious diseases significantly impact public health, with over 30,000 cancer-related deaths annually (28% of all deaths) and infectious diseases affecting hundreds of thousands. Improved vaccine and immunotherapy delivery could revolutionize treatment for these conditions, potentially saving thousands of lives and reducing healthcare costs by billions.

Our research aims to enhance drug delivery to lymph nodes, the immune system's 'command centers' where immune responses are coordinated. Current vaccines and immunotherapies often fail to reach lymph nodes efficiently, resulting in suboptimal protection against diseases.

We're developing an innovative multi-stage delivery system using DNA-based nanomaterials. This system overcomes a fundamental challenge in drug delivery: smaller materials move quickly into lymph nodes but aren't retained well, while larger materials are retained better but can't access critical areas.

Our technology dynamically changes size, utilizing DNA’s natural biodegradability to facilitate both efficient lymph node entry and effective retention. This could significantly improve vaccine and immunotherapy effectiveness for a wide range of diseases, including cancer and infectious diseases.

By enhancing vaccine design, our research could lead to more effective treatments for Ontarians, potentially reducing disease burden, improving quality of life, and strengthening the province's healthcare system and biotech industry.
Keywords: Nanotechnology, biomaterials, drug delivery, vaccines, lymph nodes, stimuli-responsive materials, supramolecular chemistry, DNA origami

Project Title: Prototype Low-Mass Dark Matter Detectors for the SNOLAB Facility
Project Description: Among modern physics’ greatest unsolved puzzles is dark matter (DM), hypothesized to constitute a quarter of the universe but to interact very feebly with the fundamental particles of visible matter. A global program of “direct detection” experiments is racing to spot DM particle interactions, using increasingly sensitive detectors in highly-shielded environments. The Super Cryogenic Dark Matter Search (SuperCDMS) is a world-leading direct detection experiment under construction in SNOLAB, Ontario’s Nobel Prize-winning underground astroparticle physics laboratory, using cryogenic semiconductor crystals with quantum sensors. The Cryogenic Underground TEst facility (CUTE) at SNOLAB is ideal for hosting the latest SuperCDMS prototypes, High-Voltage eV-sensitivity (“HVeV”) detectors. More sensitive detectors require more detailed understanding of the components’ behaviour and the environmental backgrounds. Currently, a major challenge in direct detection is understanding the source of unexpected low-energy events, inconsistent with hypothesized DM signatures, that show up in various detectors including HVeVs. This proposal will design, simulate, and fabricate improved HVeV prototypes using cutting-edge microfabrication techniques, and operate them at CUTE to characterize and minimize the low-energy excess events. Success will lay the groundwork for a breakthrough at one of SNOLAB’s flagship experiments, keeping Ontario at the forefront of astroparticle physics.
Keywords: astroparticle physics, condensed matter physics, quantum sensors, instrumentation, solid-state devices, low-background measurements, semiconductor crystals, underground laboratories, microfabrication, detector simulation

Project Title: Training Neural Networks Efficiently with Scaling Laws and Simplicity Bias
Project Description:
The Canadian government has recently announced $2.4 billion investment towards boosting the country's position in AI in the global scene. $2 billion of this funding is reserved for building and sustaining a powerful Canadian-made and controlled AI compute infrastructure, to be used to train state-of-the-art AI models. Training such models amounts to an immense amount of computation power, requiring millions of dollars worth energy, with a considerable carbon footprint. Therefore, it is of utmost importance to design training methods that take the compute budget into account.

Neural networks are at the core of modern AI and they typically have notoriously complex architectures. However, AI researchers oftentimes discover certain patterns that these models satisfy. The goal of this research program is to significantly reduce the computational cost of training an AI model by leveraging special patterns that they exhibit. My previous works discovered such patterns, and we propose to ultimately leverage these, in favor of model reusablity and principled architecture search, potentially saving immense amount of computation when training AI models. This project will contribute to Ontario’s efforts to build and sustain AI-based innovation, growth and productivity by reducing the cost of training neural networks.
Keywords: Machine Learning, Artificial Intelligence, Neural Networks, Computation, Large Language Models

Project Title: The Stellar Graveyard: a Multi-Messenger Symphony
Project Description:
When the biggest stars in the Universe reach the end of their lives, they collapse into extremely dense, invisible black holes. When two black holes crash into each other, they create ripples in spacetime that can be heard with the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observatory (of which I am a leading member). While LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA's black holes collided with one another long ago in distant galaxies, the Gaia satellite, by precisely mapping the motions of nearby stars, is revealing a population of black holes in our own galaxy, detected by their gravitational pull on their stellar companions.

The flood of observations from LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA and Gaia gives us unprecedented insight into the stellar graveyard. Recent comparison of the black holes observed has yielded two mysteries: (a) a common excess of black holes at 10 and 30 solar masses; (b) a mass gap between 2 and 10 solar masses in Gaia, which is not shared by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA's black holes.

Through a combination of data analysis and theoretical modeling, my team will tackle these mysteries, revealing their implications for stars, their explosive deaths, and cosmic chemistry. By establishing Ontario as a center for world-leading multi-messenger astrophysics research, I will attract and develop scientific talent while inspiring Ontarians.
FOR - Level 4 Sub-Class Title: General relativity and gravitational waves in astronomical and space sciences
Keywords: Gravitational waves, black holes, neutron stars, stars, galaxies, cosmology, data analysis

Project Title: The role of the pharmaceutical industry in the care of people prescribed specialty medicines: Health system and policy impacts
Project Description: High-cost specialty medicines, including biologics, represent a huge scientific advancement for the treatment of many serious chronic diseases. Specialty medicines typically cost more than $10,000 per year, and often require complicated regimens and administration. Pharmaceutical companies provide free patient support programs for people prescribed their drug only, including help with treatment adherence and free infusion care, which likely contributes to access but also the high cost of their drugs. Ontario spent over $1 billion on biologics in 2018, a 3-fold increase since 2010. The Ontario Drug Benefit program has enacted policies to switch patients to off-brand ‘biosimilars’ that are cost-effective alternatives, however, patients lose access to their patient support program and rely on biosimilar manufacturers to provide equivalent supports. Biosimilar uptake in Ontario, and Canada remains much lower than other countries. Through analysis of documents and interviews with patients, clinicians, and policymakers, this 5-year in-depth qualitative research project aims to understand the health system and policy impacts of industry patient support programs and private infusion care in Ontario and what this means for equitable access to medicines. The overarching goal is to inform sustainable pharmaceutical policy for people in Ontario prescribed specialty and biologic medicines.
Keywords: pharmaceutical policy, high cost medicines, infusion care, patient support programs, pharmaceutical industry, qualitative research, social science, health policy

Project Title: Nonviral Delivery of Gene Editors for Treating Genetic Lung Diseases
Project Description: The proposed research aims to address the severe genetic lung disease cystic fibrosis (CF), which is the most common fatal genetic disease in young Canadians with an incidence rate of ~1 in 3,600 in Ontario. CF causes thick mucus buildup in the lungs, leading to frequent infections and significant lung damage. Existing treatments are expensive, require lifelong administration, and are ineffective for patients with specific genetic mutations, particularly nonsense mutations. This project seeks to develop a long-term solution using prime editing, an advanced gene-editing technology, to correct these genetic mutations. The research involves delivering RNA-encoded prime editor components directly to the lungs through lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). The objectives are to optimize the prime editing system to correct the common CF mutation G542X, develop and screen effective LNP formulations for pulmonary delivery, and evaluate their efficacy and safety in CF mouse models. The successful implementation of this technology could vastly improve the quality of life for CF patients by offering a sustainable and effective treatment, thereby reducing long-term healthcare costs. Furthermore, this innovative approach could be extended to treat other genetic lung diseases, positioning Ontario as a pioneer in cutting-edge medical research and therapeutic development.
FOR - Level 4 Sub-Class Title: Gene and molecular therapy Gene and molecular therapy
Keywords: Nonviral gene delivery, mRNA delivery, lipid nanoparticle, nanomedicine, biomaterials, gene therapy, gene editing, prime editing, cystic fibrosis, drug delivery

Project Title: Single-Photon Imaging with Large Generative Models
Project Description: Optical imaging systems are deployed daily across Ontario: smartphone cameras capture thousands of images of everyday life, driver-assist cameras scan roadways, and satellites monitor our forests. However, existing imaging systems fail when pushed to the limits. For example, when operated at very high frame rates or in near-total darkness, conventional systems do not capture enough light to form a clear image. Within the last few years, two new imaging paradigms have emerged that promise to upend this limitation. First, "single-photon" sensors offer unprecedented light sensitivity at the individual photon level. Second, new neural networks called large generative models create photorealistic images—not by collecting photons—but through computational synthesis. These models learn from billions of images gathered from the internet and provide an unprecedented distillation of visual knowledge. The proposed research will leverage ultra-sensitive single-photon cameras and the visual knowledge of large generative models to create a new class of imaging systems that function robustly at high speeds and in ultra-low-light settings. The resulting imaging systems could have significant commercial impact in Ontario, for example, enabling new low-light imaging capabilities for hand-held photography, safer autonomous navigation systems, and improved remote sensing and monitoring of wilderness areas.
Keywords: active imaging, computational imaging, computer vision, diffusion models, generative modeling, lidar, low-light imaging, machine learning, single-photon avalanche diodes, single-photon cameras

Project Title: Gender and Political Recruitment
Project Description:
Existing research indicates that women are less likely to run for political office than men despite being equally capable of winning elections. This underrepresentation of women in politics raises concerns about achieving gender parity at all levels of government in Canada (Sevi 2021). Gendered recruitment practices, such as disproportionately encouraging men to run for office, contribute significantly to this issue, as highlighted by the Standing Committee on the Status of Women in Canada (Vecchio 2019).

The proposed research aims to address this gender gap in political recruitment, particularly focusing on Canada and Ontario, through three waves of survey experiments targeting the general population, political activists, and Ontario politicians. By analyzing responses to different recruitment messages, this study seeks to identify effective methods for encouraging women to enter politics. Additionally, the research aims to establish a causal relationship between interventions and the gender gap in recruitment, ultimately providing valuable insights for policymakers and organizations interested in fostering a more diverse candidate pool. 

The research’s outcomes, including effective recruitment strategies, broader societal shifts towards gender equality, and enhanced research capacity, promise to drive positive change and progress, fostering a more diverse, inclusive, and competitive landscape in Ontario.
Keywords: gender, political recruitment, parties, elections, representation, gender gap, experiments

Project Title: Statistical Foundations of Causal Machine Learning
Project Description:
Ontario, a global leader in machine learning (ML) with institutions like the Vector Institute and a thriving ecosystem of leading and startup AI companies, faces challenges when applying ML systems in high-stakes sectors like healthcare, justice, and finance. These critical areas demand algorithms that are not only accurate but also stable, explainable, and fair. The recent controversy surrounding Google's Gemini project exemplifies the potential pitfalls of opaque AI.

My research proposal in causal machine learning paves a promising path to trustworthy AI. It enhances traditional correlation-based approaches with causal inference. By distinguishing causation from spurious correlation, our new framework integrates causal reasoning into ML models and enhances their performance in diverse environments.

This initiative transcends academic exploration, offering real-world benefits across Ontario. By ensuring more reliable and equitable AI deployments, it has the potential to create a significant positive societal impact. It will be particularly impactful in applications like refining risk assessment models in Ontario's justice system and improving electricity price plans in Ontario. Furthermore, the program fosters collaboration between various academic disciplines, solidifying Ontario's position at the forefront of the emerging field of causal machine learning.
Keywords: Algorithmic Fairness, Causal Inference, Comparative Effectiveness Research, Distributional Robustness, Explainable AI, Generalizability, High-Dimensional Data Analysis, Trustworthy Machine Learning

Project Title: AI-Driven Sexual Abuse: Researching the Prevalence, Impact, and Solutions in Ontario
Project Description:
This research aims to delve into the growing and relatively unexplored issue of Image-Based Sexual Abuse in Ontario. The negative impact of IBSA is profound and far-reaching, inflicting severe emotional and psychological harm on victims, and causing long-term mental health consequences. This research represents a significant step forward in understanding the true extent of this issue, which has, until now, remained inadequately explored. 

The proposed study will identify the influential factors contributing to both IBSA perpetration and victimization, with a focus on higher-risk populations and their mental health outcomes. By exploring the impact of emerging AI technologies on the landscape of AI-facilitated IBSA, this research carries significant implications for policymakers, academics, and the public. The proposed study will advance knowledge creation by offering the first provincial estimate of IBSA prevalence in Canada, and push the boundaries of existing criminological theories, examining their relevance in the context of IBSA and the role of AI technology in this evolving field. 

The study project will foster multidisciplinary training, equipping students from various fields with practical research experience and promoting interdisciplinary collaboration. Findings will provide invaluable data for policymakers, enabling them to allocate resources effectively to prevent and address IBSA, ultimately enhancing public safety.
Keywords: Imaged-based sexual abuse, theory, Artificial Intelligence, revenge pornography, non-consensual sexting, sexual extortion, mental health outcomes, offending and offenders, victimization, Ontario

Project Title: Combining digital outcomes of mobility with mobile brain imaging to understand and predict future neurodegeneration
Project Description: Neurodegeneration represents a major health and economic crisis in Canada. This proposed research aims to advance our understanding of how the brain degenerates early on (up to 15 years prior to disease onset) by monitoring a person’s mobility (e.g. ranging from how stable they are on their feet to how they walk around in daily life). Mobility is fundamental to healthy aging and extremely sensitive to declining brain health. This research will identify features of declining mobility using a multi-faceted approach that will flag early neurodegeneration in people who enact their dreams (known as isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder), compared to healthy older adults and people who have early-stage Parkinson’s disease. This study will also examine the relationship between mobility impairments across these groups and the brain activity needed to control mobility, and its progression over time. This ground-breaking research will implement mobility assessments in a clinical setting whilst using state-of-the-art mobile brain imaging in addition to wearable sensors to examine free-living mobility in daily life. This project will inform clinical and digital outcomes for planning future neuroprotective trials to reduce the risk or rate of neurodegeneration. This will have significant impacts on health care and biotechnology developments in Ontario.
FOR - Level 3 Class Title: Neurosciences, medical and physiological and health aspects
Keywords: neurodegeneration; aging; Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behaviour disorder (iRBD); Parkinson's disease (PD); brain imaging; wearable technology; balance; gait; mobility; freeliving

Project Title: Revolutionizing Oncological Outcomes with Next-Generation Imaging Innovations
Project Description: This proposal introduces a revolutionary approach to enhance surgical oncology, tackling significant inefficiencies in traditional cancer tissue examination. Currently, conventional methods are slow—often taking weeks to produce results—and also risk incomplete identification of cancerous tissues. This can lead to multiple surgeries, escalating healthcare costs, and prolonged patient recovery. To address these challenges, the proposed research will advance Photon-Absorption Remote-Sensing (PARS), a revolutionary method developed and patented by the principal investigator. PARS utilizes lasers and artificial intelligence to instantly generate highly accurate images of tissues during surgery. This enables surgeons to comprehensively identify and remove all cancerous tissues in a single procedure, drastically reducing the need for additional surgeries. This method not only enhances surgical precision but also significantly cuts healthcare costs by minimizing repeat procedures. Furthermore, PARS allows for detailed molecular analysis of tissues, facilitating discovery of new biomarkers crucial for early disease detection and pharmaceutical development. Backed by over $7 million in funding, robust industry collaborations, and protected by numerous international patents, this research aims to make Ontario a global leader in medical research and innovation. The deployment of PARS is expected to improve patient outcomes dramatically and establish new healthcare standards, benefiting Ontario and the world.
Keywords: Cancer, Optics, Laser, AI, Histology, Imaging

Project Title: Developing novel biocatalysts for a sustainable environment: Reducing CO2 emission and managing plastic wastes
Project Description:
Climate change and plastic accumulation in landfills are two pressing environmental issues with far-reaching impacts. Climate change, driven by rising greenhouse gas emissions, leads to ecosystem disruptions, negatively affecting agriculture, infrastructure, and human health and concurrent plastic waste accumulation exacerbates pollution, affecting wildlife, food sources, and human health. Together, these issues create a cycle of environmental degradation, threatening biodiversity and undermining sustainable development efforts. The proposed research aims to develop eco-friendly biocatalysts for reducing CO2 emissions and managing plastic waste. Researchers will virtually screen different mutations on the catalyst proteins that may enhance their stability and functions under real-life conditions to save cost and time, and then test promising catalysts in lab through biochemical experiments.  

Implementing enzyme-based CO2 capture can help Ontario industries meet stringent emissions targets, reducing the province's carbon footprint and contributing to global climate change mitigation efforts. Additionally, enzymatic degradation of plastic can reduce the accumulation of plastic waste in landfills, promoting a circular economy by converting waste into valuable resources. These technologies will complement the Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food, and Rural Affairs’s bio-based initiatives, enhancing Ontario’s environmental stewardship and driving sustainable economic growth, creating new jobs, and training next-generation scientists in cutting-edge technologies.
Keywords: Enzyme, Biocatalyst, CO2 capture, Plastic biodegradation, environment sustainability, protein engineering, molecular modeling and dynamics, stability and activity, language models

Project Title: Broadening Connections between Robustness and Privacy
Project Description: Both privacy and robustness are critical considerations in modern data analysis and essential components of any trustworthy machine learning system handling real people’s data. Improving our understanding of these considerations is particularly time-sensitive given that new legislation (e.g., Bill C-27) mandating additional care in terms of privacy is being introduced. The proposed research seeks to broaden our understanding of connections between robustness and privacy in machine learning and statistics. The PI's recent work has demonstrated fundamental connections between these two properties. The proposed research will design improved algorithms that exploit such connections and broaden the scope in adjacent, more challenging and more realistic settings than previously considered. For example, improved algorithms would preserve privacy and ensure robustness in settings where individuals may each possess sizable sensitive datasets, or in settings where the goal may be to predict labels for datapoints, or draw new datapoints which resemble a sensitive dataset. The proposed research will result in new algorithms, methods, and techniques for these settings, enhancing our understanding of privacy-preserving statistical techniques. This will allow Ontario organizations across various industries (e.g., technology, finance, healthcare, etc.) to modernize and ensure compliance, resulting in better data protection for all Ontarians.
FOR - Level 3 Class Title: Theoretical computer science and computational mathematics
Keywords: differential privacy, robustness, algorithms, statistics, estimation

Project Title: A novel device for treating otitis media
Project Description:
Tympanostomy is the most common surgery performed on children and is the standard clinical treatment for chronic and recurring otitis media. Otitis media (infection and/or accumulation of liquid in the middle-ear space) is a common childhood disease and the second most prevalent cause of hearing loss and the leading cause of health care visits and antibiotic prescriptions. Between 2005 and 2018, Ontario had over eight million cases of acute otitis media alone. Tympanostomy involves inserting a ventilation tube after making a slit in the tympanic membrane.

Successful tympanostomy requires holding the patient’s head stationary, necessitating general anesthesia in children. Tympanostomy has other drawbacks such as long-term damage to the tympanic membrane and economic burden due to surgery and other medical and indirect costs. In this project, the PI will develop a paradigm-shifting microneedle-patch device for low-risk treatment of otitis media. An interdisciplinary approach will enable the development and preclinical validation of this device that will overcome drawbacks of tympanostomy.  In addition to its impact on health in Ontario, this device will bring new opportunities for the medical device sector in Ontario because it will open the huge international market of otitis media treatment valued at USD 7.65 billion in 2030.
Keywords: tympanic membrane, middle ear, hearing, vibration, ear infection, tympanostomy, myringotomy, otology, microneedle, ventilation tube

Project Title: Advancing the next generation of artificial leaves for carbon dioxide reduction
Project Description: To address rising CO2 emissions and the need for clean energy, researchers have developed artificial leaves that mimic the ability of natural leaves to capture CO2 and convert it into usable energy (sugars for plants). Unlike natural leaves, however, artificial leaves transform CO2 into sustainable fuels and chemicals that people can use to power homes, workplaces, and industries. Although this groundbreaking technology is full of potential, at this early stage of development, barriers preventing the widescale industrial adoption of this technology include: 1) low conversion efficiency and high energy consumption required for CO2 recovery, and 2) real flue gas conversion has not been demonstrated in the lab. The proposed research will leverage Dr. Wu’s experience and collaborations to conduct in situ multimodal characterization to refine strain-engineered catalysts for flue gas conversion and integrated reactive carbon capture to improve conversion efficiency. This research will advance the technology of artificial leaves using mechanical energy and solid electrolytes in a novel flow reactor to improve the energy efficiency of CO2 conversion. This novel technology has the potential to mitigate climate change through the reduction of CO2 emissions, and provide Ontario with clean renewable energy and a large-scale energy storage strategy.
FOR - Level 4 Sub-Class Title: Electrical, optical, catalytic, and magnetic properties of thin layers
Keywords: CO2 reduction, high entropy alloy, electrocatalysis, reactive carbon capture, flow reactor, machine learning, clean energy, catalyst, energy materials

Project Title: Advanced Real-Time Visual Inspection for Lifeline Infrastructure
Project Description: Canada's lifeline infrastructure, including bridges, pipelines, and towers, constructed during the mid-20th century, is now approaching or has already reached the end of its design life. This research addresses these aging infrastructure challenges by developing an innovative vision-based inspection system using robotics and artificial intelligence (AI). Focusing on telecommunication towers as proof of concept, the project aims to create a scalable and practical solution to address the pressing need for improved infrastructure maintenance and safety. The proposed system employs a collaborative path planning algorithm for multiple drones to ensure efficient image capture, which is then used to generate detailed 3D models through Novel View Synthesis technology. This allows on-site inspectors to virtually explore structures and rapidly identify areas of concern. By incorporating AI-powered image recognition and anomaly detection, the system can automatically identify changes or irregularities in structures over time, streamlining the inspection process and enabling more effective management of Canada's infrastructure. For Ontario, which faces the highest infrastructure replacement costs among provinces, this innovation could yield significant benefits, including substantial cost savings, enhanced public safety, and more efficient management of critical infrastructure, potentially extending their lifespan.
FOR - Level 2 Group Title: Civil engineering, maritime engineering, transport engineering, and mining engineering
Keywords: Structure Inspection, Smart Structure, Computer Vision, Robotic Inspection, Anomaly Detection, Human-machine Interaction, Real-time Processing

Project Title: Heritage beyond the White City: Reclaiming Heritage as Community Stewardship
Project Description:
Heritage preservation continues to disproportionately negatively impact racialized and working-class neighbourhoods because traditional heritage practices focus on architectural integrity, aesthetic unity and social order (the virtues of Daniel Burnham’s White City) and ignore community expertise and citizen participation (whose heritage). This results in heritage practices perpetuating socioeconomic divides, reinforcing the exclusion and displacement of the communities they are meant to serve. To better serve all communities, heritage practices must address those historically underserved. Starting from Toronto’s Chinatown West (pilot site), the research will develop new digital tools and platforms to expand heritage practices to include and mobilize existing legacy and strategies of community organizing, community ownership, and community stewardship. Specifically, we will build a collaborative and community-controlled digital platform to facilitate citizen participation and empower residents to actively steward their heritage. In collaboration with the Toronto Chinatown Land Trust (TCLT), the initiative will leverage local knowledge and develop new tools and methodologies to expand heritage practices for social justice. 

The research will benefit Ontario by demonstrating how inclusive, community-driven approaches can lead to sustainable heritage preservation and community asset management. This project will serve as a model for other underserved neighbourhoods, promoting equitable and resilient urban futures across the province.
FOR - Level 2 Group Title: Arts (arts, history of arts, performing arts, music), architecture and design
Keywords: architectural heritage, community heritage, community memory, community land trust, community ownership, co-design, participatory action research, digital art, imagination, techno-orientalism

Project Title: Coding with AI: Enhancing Software Development through Visual Interfaces
Project Description: The advent of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language models (LLMs) has initiated a paradigm shift in how people write, reuse, and debug code in software development and related industries. Despite many benefits due to automated code generation, there exist numerous challenges that we must address when integrating LLMs into current software development workflows, such as misalignment between developers’ intents and generated code, insufficient support for managing conversations with AI, obstacles in collaborative programming tasks, and difficulty in understanding and integrating code created by AI. These challenges all boil down to the significant gap between humans and AI, which is yet to be addressed with robust visual interfaces. This research aims to innovate more holistic, smooth, and versatile LLM-powered programming environments by leveraging novel human-in-the-loop interactive visualization techniques. It will approach the goal by augmenting four key aspects in developers’ workflows—preparation, execution, cooperation, and dissemination—with the power of interactive visualization that offers effective sense-making and direct manipulation of abstract concepts, models, and data. The outcomes of this research will impact Ontario’s billion-dollar software and computer service industries with cutting-edge scientific achievement and the recruitment, retention, and training of talents.
Keywords: information visualization, human-computer interaction, human-AI interaction, programming support, large language models, sense-making, externalization, direct manipulation, collaboration, computational narrative

Project Title: The Road Less Traveled: Exploring the Intersection of Driving, Cannabis, and the Experiences of Racialized Youth in Ontario
Project Description: For the last 30 years, motor vehicle collisions, most of which involve alcohol and/or drugs, have been the leading cause of death for Canadians between the ages of 15 to 24. More youth than ever before are driving under the influence of cannabis (DUIC), more so than alcohol. Decades of educational and prevention strategies have contributed to reductions in alcohol-impaired driving, yet DUIC is on the rise. This risk is further compounded for racialized Canadian youth, who have historically experienced unequal police surveillance and drug enforcement and whose voices have been dramatically underrepresented in cannabis related research. Therefore, DUIC interventions risk overlooking the experiences of racialized youth and further perpetuating stigmatizing and colonizing views of risk and behavior change.
