With the guidance of our youth collaborative board, this research will expand my current CIHR funded study (2023-2026) investigating youth’s (ages 14 to 24) DUIC risk profiles, by focusing on the individual and social DUIC determinants of racialized Ontario youth. My findings will inform future collaborative youth-led DUIC interventions that foreground the voices of racialized youth. Understanding what influences youth DUIC will enable us to stop it. The voices of racialized youth are needed, and their silencing through underrepresentation must end.

Project Title: Pathway-specific kinase substrates in plant immunity & development
Project Description: Plants must sense and respond to their environment to survive. Receptor kinases (RKs) are the primary sensors at the plant cell surface, where they perceive extracellular stimuli and activate intracellular signal transduction pathways to trigger appropriate cellular/physiological responses, thereby controlling essentially all aspects of plant life. Many RKs and their ligands have been identified that regulate growth, development, reproduction, immunity, and abiotic stress responses; however, the intracellular signalling mechanisms downstream of most RKs remain unknown, representing a critical knowledge gap and hindering the development of improved traits in crops. The DeFalco lab is using a multidisciplinary approach to study how RKs trigger specific responses to extracellular stimuli. We are particularly focused on the cytosolic protein kinases that associate with RK complexes to activate pathway-specific signalling via phosphorylation and regulation of substrate proteins. This proposal aims to characterize signalling networks that mediate pathway-specific responses downstream of RKs, as well as apply this knowledge to engineering novel signaling circuits in plants. By elucidating the molecular mechanisms of RK/RLCK signaling pathways, particularly in the context of immunity and development, we seek to identify novel components and engineer improved stress tolerance and disease resistance in crops, addressing critical issues in agriculture and food security.
Keywords: receptor kinases; phosphorylation; kinase substrates; signal tranduction; plant immunity; plant development; peptide signalling; receptor-like cytoplasmic kinases

Project Title: GENIUS: A GENerative artificial Intelligence framework to Uncover the neural mechanismS of image memorability
Project Description:
In today's visually rich world, some images stand out and stick in our minds, a phenomenon called image memorability. My research seeks to understand why certain images are more memorable, identify the brain signals that predict this, and develop AI systems that can enhance image memorability and human memory performance by altering photographs.

By combining advanced AI with cognitive neuroscience, we aim to reveal the brain processes behind image memorability and how these processes can be influenced. This research has practical applications in education, media, and healthcare. Understanding how the brain remembers images can help create better learning tools for students, develop strategies to support people with memory issues like dementia, and improve overall mental health outcomes.

Ontario faces an alarming rise in dementia cases, with a projected 202% increase from 2020 to 2050. By mid-century, Ontario will have the highest number of new cases in Canada, totalling ~2.9 million. This surge highlights the urgent need for advanced research into human memory and innovative solutions to tackle this public health crisis. This research can lead to improved support for individuals with memory impairments, and significant advancements in mental health care, thereby enhancing the quality of life for countless Ontarians.

Project Title: Virtual navigation tasks and memory consolidation during human intracranial clinical recordings
Project Description: Imagine your brain as a network of cities, each responsible for storing different aspects of a memory. During sleep, these cities exchange resources to hold on to the most important memories from the day. In recent work, I found that these "cities" do not activate and deactivate at the same time to complete this task; rather, they turn on and off in a complex wave of communication (Muller et al., eLife, 2016). We will collaborate with a team of neurologists and neurosurgeons at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) to understand how this wave helps to store memories in coordinated assemblies across the human brain. In collaboration with LHSC, we have developed a new memory task that can be administered during intracranial recordings in the neurosurgery clinic. Using new computational algorithms I have developed, we will map traveling waves in the brain as subjects sleep, after learning a virtual reality (VR) navigation environment. Results from this work will solidify a collaboration between LHSC and Western University as an internationally recognized centre for computational neuroscience and memory research. Both the applications of this research and the HQP trained in this work will directly benefit Ontario's knowledge economy and growing neurotechnology sector.
Keywords: Computational neuroscience, sleep, human memory, memory consolidation, algorithms for neural data, data science

Project Title: Quantum Photonics in Neuroimaging: Sensing Brain-Generated Light towards Early Detection of Brain Disease
Project Description: Mental health disorders affect about one in five Ontarians with rates of new diagnoses rising rapidly each year, necessitating urgent advancements in brain imaging for earlier detection. Dr. Murugan’s research program leverages new findings that suggest brain cells may communicate using light that arises from metabolic reactions, which travel faster than the well-known electrochemical signals, through tissues without direct connections. This research aims to 1) understand how neurons guide light, similar to fiber optic cables, and 2) to use quantum sensors to detect ultra-early, functional changes in brain states using these natural light emissions. Armed with this new knowledge, the long-term goal of this work is to leverage advances in quantum optics to not only understand the fundamentals of neural communication but also develop commercializable quantum sensing technologies that will ultimately improve long-term brain health, and position Ontario as a leader advancing health technology and in quantum innovation.
Keywords: Quantum sensing, brain imaging, optical communication, ultra-weak photon emission, biophysics, non-invasive, neural waveguides, neurophysiology, non-chemical signaling, photonics

Project Title: Understanding disparities and improving outcomes for patients with lobular breast cancer.
Project Description: The proposed research aims to better understand why patients with lobular breast cancer have worse survival than patients with ductal breast cancer. Using administrative health care data at ICES Ontario, we will study the impact of social determinants of health, provider and treatment center characteristics, and treatment and practice patterns on survival. The knowledge generated from these population-level data may inform health policy and interventions directed at improving access to breast cancer screening and awareness and education efforts amongst providers treating lobular breast cancer. We will, in parallel, perform a multicenter, pan-Canadian observational cohort study of patients with lobular breast cancer, systematically collecting sociodemographic, tumour, treatment, and outcomes (i.e. survival, recurrence) data. This study will allow us to determine the best treatment strategies (e.g. diagnostic, surgery, systemic) for lobular breast cancer. The knowledge generated from these studies may spur the development of best-practice clinical guidelines for lobular breast cancer. This research program benefits Ontario by improving the health outcomes of patients with lobular breast cancer, by training highly qualified personnel such as research coordinators, graduate students, and post-doctoral research fellows, and positions the PI as an international leader in lobular breast cancer.

Project Title: Bridging the Gap: Integrating Non-Human Primate Models, AI, and Human Phenotypes to Understand Sensory Processing in Autism
Project Description: This research aims to uncover the brain mechanisms behind atypical sensory processing in autism spectrum disorder (ASD), addressing how individuals with autism experience the world differently, particularly in visual information processing. Our innovative approach uniquely combines computer models of the brain with precise neural manipulations of monkey brains to simulate and better understand the neural underpinnings of autism-like behaviors, introducing controlled "noise" into specific brain regions to test its effects on sensory processing. This work aligns with Ontario's commitment to supporting individuals with autism, as evidenced by the recent $120 million allocation to the Ontario Autism Program. Moreover, our project has significant potential to benefit community organizations serving individuals with ASD, for which the Ontario government has allocated $310 million over three years to address increasing operational costs. Our research will provide these organizations with optimized experimental designs, improved diagnostic tools, and novel intervention strategies, helping them deliver more effective and efficient services. This, in turn, maximizes the impact of the government's investment in community support. By advancing our understanding of autism, we aim to improve the quality of life for Ontarians with autism and their families, while positioning Ontario as a leader in translational autism research.

Project Title: Improving the effectiveness and mobilization of wildfire predictive services to enhance community safety

Predictive services (PS) are critical tools that bring together multi-disciplinary experts and specialists to provide essential fire behaviour modelling, fire weather forecasting, and other forms of prediction to support response, resource allocation, and the protection of life, communities, infrastructure, and the environment. While PS are already adopted in many regions highly impacted by wildfire (e.g., British Columbia, Canada; Victoria, Australia), they face many limitations when it comes to effectively supporting operations. Moreover, in Ontario, such a unit does not exist, and these functions are scattered through different silos in Ontario Aviation, Forest Fire, and Emergency Services (AFFES), the provincial agency responsible for managing wildfire. This project is co-designed, co-created, and supported by AFFES based on their need to enhance their implementation of predictive services. This research will explore best practices in overcoming challenges in PS through in-depth case studies of PS units around the world, interviews with key stakeholders in Ontario, and reviews of both academic and grey literature.
